newsitem.title: SPAIN: Second Spanish paper prints "dirty war" documents.
newsitem.headline: Second Spanish paper prints "dirty war" documents.

text.p: A second major Spanish newspaper has published leaked papers purporting to prove the former Socialist administration set up death squads which waged a "dirty war" against Basque separatist rebels in the 1980s.

The pro-Socialist El Pais on Tuesday printed the entire set of 20 documents demanded by courts investigating the state's role in the "dirty war", one day after pro-conservative El Mundo published the first four papers.
Attorney General Juan Ortiz Urculo said on Monday that the documents could provide evidence for reopening a high-level investigation of former government officials.

Courts are demanding the declassification of the documents and the government has refused citing reasons of state security. The Supreme Court is due to rule early next year on whether the government can be forced to hand them over.
But deputy Prime Minister Francisco Alvarez Cascos said on Tuesday the government had not changed its position and would not now be pressured into declassifying the documents.
"As I know the government cannot be pressured, it doesn't surprise me that this has had not persuaded us to change our stance," Cascos told journalists at a press conference.

High officials and former security chiefs under the 13-year Socialist tenure have been charged with running death squads known as the Anti-Terrorist Liberation Groups (GAL), which killed 28 people in 1983-87, many of them in southern France.
The allegations contributed to the election defeat last March of former Socialist prime minister Felipe Gonzalez to the conservative Popular Party government of Jose Maria Aznar.
Supreme Court judges probing the death squads voted six to four last month against questioning Gonzalez, who denies involvement, but left the way open to reverse the decision if new evidence emerged.
El Pais said all of the papers referred to the "dirty war" against ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) guerrillas and were found in court briefs on the GAL case.

But the newspaper said it did not know if the documents were authentic, saying they had been found during a court search of the prison cell of ex-spy Juan Alberto Perote, who claimed to have stolen them from Spain's military intelligence agency CESID.
Defence Minister Eduardo Serra told journalists in Brussels, however, that he believed the published documents were very similar to those held by the courts.

Perote, one of those charged in the GAL case, tried to hide the papers in the prison library and also tried to eat some of them while his cell was being searched. He later leaked the documents to El Mundo.
El Mundo said the papers directly demonstrated that CESID set up GAL and selected the first victim: alleged ETA rebel Ramon Onederra.
